_comment: Everything the scanner needs to know about a warehouse. Derived from
warehouse/warehouse.yaml; the field-by-field mapping is in the README.
Nothing here is baked into scanner.py, so a new warehouse is a new file.
Coordinates are Gazebo world coordinates, metres. Yaw follows MAVSDK:
0 is north (+Y), positive is clockwise, so +90 faces +X and -90 faces -X.
A face is given by the x of the shelf surface itself, not by the aisle
centre line. Where the vehicle flies follows from face_x and standoff,
which lets it stand closer to the shelf than the middle of the aisle.
That matters here: the real C27 hires stream is 1024x768, and at the
1.216 m aisle centre a 2.8 mm module resolves to 2.04 px, below the 3 px
a QR needs. At 0.80 m it is 3.10 px.
The aisles in this warehouse taper: 2.40, 1.77, 1.13 and 0.50 m of clear
width. Standoff is therefore per face, not one number for the building.
Aisles 1 and 2 are wide enough to hold the 0.80 m the camera wants; in
aisles 3 and 4 the vehicle can only fly the centre line, so standoff is
half the aisle. A face falls back to shelf_standoff when it names none.
READ THIS BEFORE FLYING. The x500 is 0.648 m across (rotor hub 0.174 +
propeller radius 0.150, so 0.324 m either side of centre). Against the
half-widths above that leaves 0.876, 0.561, 0.241 and -0.074 m of side
clearance. Aisle 3 is inside waypoint_tolerance, which is 0.40 m, so the
vehicle can be commanded onto the racking there. Aisle 4 is narrower
than the vehicle: faces G and H cannot be flown at all. Both are left
in the route rather than quietly dropped, because a scan that silently
skips a quarter of the warehouse reads as a scan that found nothing
there. The vehicle size was not changed to fit; the aisle was narrowed
under it on purpose.
_shelf_standoff_note: Fallback for a face that names no standoff of its own. Every face here
does, so this is only the default for a hand-written layout.
_ground_offset_note: How far base_link, and therefore the camera, rests above the floor when
the vehicle is landed. Commanded altitudes are relative to the spawn
point, which is captured on the ground, so without this every commanded
height is this much too high in world terms. Measured by back-computing
the camera height from decoded labels of known position: +0.221, +0.232
and +0.227 m at the three shelf levels.
It cost 63 percent of a scan. Labels sat 0.16 to 0.26 m below the optical
axis instead of on it, so only the topmost of the three box heights fell
inside the 0.234 m half-frame; the other two read 22 and 0 percent.
_merge_note: The warehouse comes from warehouse_ibrahim; the vehicle from
starling2_furkan. ground_offset is the airframe's, not the building's:
0.060 for the Starling 2 where the x500 measured 0.227.
vehicle_half_span is 0.145, half of the Starling's 290 mm across the
propeller tips. The aisle table's flyable flags are recomputed from it,
which changes the narrowest aisle: an x500 does not fit in 0.50 m and a
Starling does, with 105 mm a side. Whether that is enough to fly is a
separate question from whether it fits.
_camera_reach_note: How far each camera reads, measured by standoff_sweep.py on real label
textures rendered at the size and obliquity each distance gives, asking
for reliability out to 25 degrees off axis because a code sweeps across
the whole frame as the vehicle passes it.
These place the lane in an aisle of any width: both distances must add
up to the width and each must stay inside its camera's reach, so the
width is split between them in proportion to these two numbers.
An aisle wider than the two together cannot be read from one lane and
costs a pass a face instead.
